hero.title: Lifebox
hero.lead: An experiment in whether an app's interface can be shaped for each person who uses it, instead of one design for everyone. It is planned as Atti's phone app.

image.alt: Lifebox's Now screen for Alex and Blair, the app's two sample people, side by side. Alex sees four things as large cards with action buttons, starting with dog food. Blair sees three compact rows with check circles, starting with concert tickets.

figure.caption: The same Now screen for two people: one app, assembled from each person's data.

sections.title: Memory adapts too
paragraphs: Alex's Memory opens on recent purchases. Blair's opens on saved places.
Both are the app's built-in sample people, running the same code.

image.alt: Alex's Memory screen in Lifebox, sample data. It opens on Recent purchases: dog food and running shoes, then Coming up: a concert.
Blair's Memory screen in Lifebox, sample data. It opens on Saved places, such as a bakery and a coffee shop, then Upcoming: a concert and a birthday dinner.

sections.title: Where it's at
paragraphs: An Expo and React Native app. You drop in short notes, and it turns them into structured memories and events, looks for patterns, and brings back what matters in a feed called Now. It is not released, and the hardest problem, shipping a different build to each person, is still open.

facts.caption: Each app is tuned for one person, so there is no crowd to average over.
One iOS build and release, which this design needs per person.

sections.label: Details
sections.stepsLabel: Personal, then popular, then community, then core
sections.text: When a personal change keeps winning for several people who opted in, it could become a candidate default, climbing from personal to popular to community to core. An idea, not built.

feature.title: Grow your own app
feature.text: You tell the app what you want in your own words. When the change fits the layout settings it already has, it makes it right away and keeps an Undo. Anything else can be sent on as an idea for a later build.

expanders.title: What I'm building
paragraphs: One codebase, with a different configuration for each person. The frame of the app stays stable and the content adapts: what shows on Now, in what order, and how dense it is. Every change is visible, explained in one line, and can be undone. The app only accepts configuration that passes a schema; it never runs code an AI wrote.

expanders.title: What I tried
paragraphs: I wrote a design paper, "Stable Frame, Adaptive Content", on what may adapt and how to test a change when the sample is one person. It sets two rules: judge a change from week three, and drop the first days of each test block so novelty doesn't count as success. I explored four visual directions for the Now screen. Lifebox's rules for reading dates and intents in plain text now also run inside Atti. I also studied AI tools that generate website variants and keep whatever converts. Their loop carries over: generate, constrain, measure, keep what works. Their statistics don't.

expanders.title: What didn't work
paragraphs: Releases. Apps ship one release to everybody, and one iOS build takes 30 to 60 minutes. A separate one for each person is the whole point here, and no approach to that works yet. Crowd-style testing doesn't work either: one person gives a few signals a week, too few to split, so layout changes must never be tested that way.

expanders.title: Open questions and next
paragraphs: Can Atti propose one change at a time from what my personal brain already knows, and can the brain guide those choices without its contents leaving my machine? When a personal change keeps winning for several people who opted in, it could become a candidate default, climbing from personal to popular to community to core. And who approves a low-risk change: the user each time, or Atti on its own once they opt in?
